data.name: New Zealand
data.summary: New Zealand has no general capital gains tax, no inheritance, estate or gift tax and no net wealth tax, but a resident holding more than NZD 50,000 (cost) of foreign shares is taxed under the foreign investment fund (FIF) rules: normally 5% of the opening market value is deemed income (fair dividend rate), taxed at up to 39%, i.e. about 1.95% of the portfolio's value a year whatever the actual return (individuals may use the actual total return instead when it is lower, never below zero). Dividends and gains on those shares are not taxed separately. New residents get a once-only 4-year transitional-resident exemption on most foreign investment income, and since 2025 some new migrants can elect a realisation-based revenue account method (dividends plus 70% of gains), which US citizens can apply to all their foreign shares. Gains on residential property sold within 2 years (bright-line test) or on assets bought for resale are taxed.

regimes.name: New Zealand tax resident
regimes.description: Worldwide income taxed at up to 39% (above NZD 180,000); foreign portfolio shares taxed under the FIF rules.
regimes.eligibility: Resident with a permanent place of abode in New Zealand or after more than 183 days in any 12-month period.

capital_gains.summary: No comprehensive capital gains tax. Gains are taxed only where property was acquired for the purpose of disposal, in a profit-making scheme, by dealers, or on residential land sold within the 2-year bright-line period (main home excluded). Gains on foreign shares are not taxed on sale for a resident above the FIF threshold because the FIF regime taxes a deemed 5% return each year instead (recorded under wealth_tax).
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Bright-line test: residential land disposed of within 2 years of acquisition (disposals on or after 1 July 2024; previously up to 10 years). Main home exclusion.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Income Tax Act 2007 s CB 3/CB 4: gains on personal property (including shares) acquired with a dominant purpose of disposal are taxable at marginal rates. Financial arrangements (bonds, foreign-currency deposits) are taxed on accrual including FX gains. FIF holders leaving New Zealand are deemed to dispose of FIF interests at market value for FIF purposes.

capital_gains.rate_basis: No CGT for a long-term investor without a purpose of resale; local real estate outside the 2-year bright-line period. Foreign listed shares: 0% on sale because the FIF FDR method (modelled as a 1.95% annual levy in wealth_tax) replaces taxation of gains and dividends.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Share or property dealers, and anyone who acquired an asset for the dominant purpose of resale, are taxed on gains at marginal rates up to 39%. Purpose is a factual test; frequent trading is a risk.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: 2-year bright-line for residential land; no holding rule for shares.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Foreign shares above NZD 50,000 total cost: FIF regime (see wealth_tax). ASX-listed Australian resident companies that keep a franking account are exempt from FIF; their dividends are taxed, gains are not.

dividends.summary: New Zealand dividends carry imputation credits (company rate 28%); a top-rate shareholder pays 39% on the grossed-up dividend less the credit, about 15.3% of a fully imputed cash dividend. Foreign dividends on FIF interests valued under the FDR method are not taxed separately (the 5% deemed return replaces them). Below the NZD 50,000 de minimis, foreign dividends are taxed at up to 39% with a foreign tax credit.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: FIF de minimis: total cost of attributing foreign interests NZD 50,000 or less.
dividends.important_exceptions: Australian franking credits are not usable in New Zealand. Foreign tax credits are limited to the treaty rate (e.g. 15%).

dividends.rate_basis: Domestic: fully imputed dividend D, taxable D/0.72, tax 39% x D/0.72 = 0.542D less credit 0.389D = 0.153D. Foreign: 0 because under FDR the dividends are subsumed in the 5% deemed return taxed under wealth_tax (1.95% of value); source WHT is credited against the FIF tax. A small portfolio (under NZD 50,000 cost) would pay 39% on foreign dividends instead.
dividends.withholding_outbound: NRWT on dividends: 0% on fully imputed dividends to 10%+ holders, 15% on fully imputed cash dividends to portfolio holders, 30% otherwise (treaty-reduced).
dividends.treaty_network: About 41 treaties (PwC table), including the US (15% portfolio dividends), Australia, UK and major EU states.
dividends.holding_company_notes: Company tax 28% with imputation. A New Zealand company holding the foreign portfolio pays FIF tax at 28% instead of 39% and is modelled as the 'investment_company' structure regime. Portfolio investment entities (PIEs) cap investor tax at 28% with no further tax on distributions, but a family cannot normally set up its own PIE (investor-number and other eligibility rules), so this applies to investing through public PIE funds rather than to a family vehicle.

wealth_tax.summary: No net wealth tax. However, the FIF fair dividend rate method taxes 5% of the opening market value of foreign shares each year as income (39% top rate = about 1.95% of value), regardless of actual dividends or gains. It is recorded here as a limited levy on foreign financial assets because economically it works like one.
wealth_tax.exemptions_thresholds: Applies only if the total cost of foreign attributing interests exceeds NZD 50,000 at any time in the year. Exempt: ASX-listed Australian-resident companies with franking accounts. Individuals and eligible family trusts may instead pay on the actual total return (comparative value) when it is lower than 5%, and the portfolio total cannot go below zero.
wealth_tax.important_exceptions: Statutory basis: Income Tax Act 2007 subpart EX (FIF rules), FDR method. Budget 2026 proposals (IRD information sheet, 28 May 2026; not yet law, bill status not confirmed): all residents could use the revenue account method for unlisted foreign shares only, residents taxed twice because of citizenship or a right to work elsewhere (mainly US citizens) could use the extended RAM for all foreign shares, and the FIF de minimis would rise from NZD 50,000 to NZD 100,000 from 1 April 2026 if enacted. A listed portfolio held by an EU family stays under the FDR method.

components.name: FIF fair dividend rate (5% deemed return taxed at 39%)
components.notes: Threshold is on total cost, not value, and is not indexed (set in 2000; IRD's Budget 2026 information sheet proposes raising it from NZD 50,000 to NZD 100,000). Rate = 5% x 39% top marginal rate. Foreign source dividend WHT is creditable against it. In loss or low-return years individuals can pay on the actual return (comparative value), floor zero.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Local council rates on land based on rateable value. No stamp duty on property. Residential land withholding tax applies to offshore sellers within the bright-line period.

inheritance.summary: No inheritance, estate or gift tax. Estate duty was abolished in 1992 and gift duty for transfers made on or after 1 October 2011 (Inland Revenue's gift duty abolition note and gifting overview, found by search and not opened). Transfers to children are tax-free; for FIF shares the heirs simply continue under the FIF rules.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Inherited residential land is generally outside the bright-line test for the heir (general rule; not verified). Trusts: trustee income tax rate 39% from 2024/25 (not verified in this session).

regimes.name: Transitional resident (4-year exemption)
regimes.description: New migrants and New Zealanders returning after 10 years are exempt for about 4 years on most foreign income: foreign interest, dividends, FIF income, rent and gains. Foreign employment and personal-services income is not exempt.
regimes.eligibility: Became tax resident on or after 1 April 2006, not tax resident at any time in the previous 10 years, never transitional before. Ends 4 years after the end of the month of qualifying, or earlier on opting out (e.g. claiming Working for Families credits). Automatic; opting out is irrevocable.

capital_gains.summary: Foreign-source gains (e.g. on foreign shares) are exempt during the transitional period; New Zealand-source gains taxed as for residents (generally none).

regimes.name: Revenue account method for new migrants (extended RAM for foreign citizens taxed abroad, e.g. US citizens)
regimes.description: Introduced on 30 March 2026 (IRD, Budget 2026 information sheet), eligible new residents who became resident on or after 1 April 2024 after at least five years of non-residence may elect to tax qualifying FIF shares on a realisation basis: dividends at marginal rates plus 70% of realised gains. Under 'extended RAM' it applies to all foreign shares of a person who remains liable to tax on their disposal in another country by citizenship or right to live there (in practice US citizens). Leaving New Zealand triggers a deferred deemed disposal for 3 years.
regimes.eligibility: Natural person (or family trust whose principal settlor qualifies) who became resident (not transitional) on or after 1 April 2024 after at least five years of non-residence. Without the extended rule RAM covers only unlisted foreign shares acquired before arrival, so for a listed portfolio it is relevant mainly to US citizens.
regimes.duration_note: RAM is an election, not a time-limited concession: once a qualifying migrant elects it, it keeps applying to the elected FIF interests while the person remains resident; it ends only on leaving New Zealand (deemed disposal, deferred for 3 years).

capital_gains.summary: Gains on RAM foreign shares are taxed on sale at 70% x marginal rate = 27.3% at the 39% rate; losses only offset RAM gains/dividends.

dividends.summary: Dividends on RAM shares are taxed when received at marginal rates (39% top) with a foreign tax credit.

regimes.name: New Zealand investment holding company (28% company tax on FIF income)
regimes.description: The family's foreign portfolio is held by a New Zealand company. Under the foreign investment fund (FIF) rules the company is taxed on a deemed 5% return (fair dividend rate) at the 28% company rate, 1.4% of value a year, instead of 1.95% at the 39% personal rate. Actual dividends and gains on the foreign shares are not taxed separately; New Zealand has no general capital gains tax. Distributions to the family carry imputation credits for the 28% already paid, leaving 11 points to pay at the 39% rate.
regimes.eligibility: Any New Zealand-resident family once the 4-year transitional-resident exemption is over (during it, holding personally is better: foreign investment income is exempt for the individual but not for a New Zealand company). Not useful for US persons (the company is a PFIC/CFC for US tax) or for migrants using the revenue account method, which only natural persons and family trusts can elect.
regimes.duration_note: Ordinary company taxation with no time limit; it lasts as long as the company holds the portfolio and the family stays resident.

structure.entity: New Zealand limited company (investment holding company)
structure.payout_notes: Dividends are taxable to resident shareholders with imputation credits for company tax paid: at the 39% rate, a fully imputed dividend D costs 39% x D/0.72 - 0.389D = 15.3% of the cash. The company's FIF income (5% of a foreign portfolio of roughly NZD 50 million, about NZD 2.5 million a year) generates enough imputation credits to fully impute the family's withdrawals. Cash paid out of untaxed surpluses (actual returns above the deemed 5%) carries no credits and is taxed at 39%, except that realised capital gains can be paid out tax-free on liquidation (s CD 26 / CD 44, BR Pub 14/09). Resident withholding tax applies to dividends at 33% less imputation credits; shareholder loans need market interest.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Running cost is a reasoned estimate, not sourced (annual financial statements, company income tax return with FIF and imputation calculations, Companies Office annual return). A company must use the fair dividend rate (or other prescribed) method: it cannot switch to the comparative value method in years when the actual return is below 5%, has no NZD 50,000 de minimis, and cannot claim FIF losses, so in bad years it pays 1.4% while an individual could pay 0. ASX-listed Australian companies are outside the FIF rules; their dividends are taxed to the company with franking not creditable. Gains on shares held for resale are taxable income (dealer test). The general anti-avoidance rule (s BG 1, Penny and Hooper) targets arrangements that divert personal income into a company; holding a passive portfolio in a company is a long-accepted choice, but the 2024 increase of the trustee rate to 39% came with integrity rules on income routed through close companies (s HC 38, not verified). The trustee rate itself is 39%, so a family trust offers no rate advantage.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: New Zealand has no exit tax for individuals emigrating; the company stays resident while managed in New Zealand. On liquidation, subscribed capital and realised capital gains are returned tax-free, and the rest (including retained FIF income) is a dividend with imputation credits. Dividends paid to shareholders who have become non-resident bear non-resident withholding tax (rates not verified here).

income.name: New Zealand

income_tax.summary: Residents pay 10.5% to NZD 15,600, 17.5% to NZD 53,500, 30% to NZD 78,100, 33% to NZD 180,000 and 39% above; there is no general social security tax. Employees pay the ACC earners' levy of 1.75% up to NZD 156,641; KiwiSaver (3.5% default) is not compulsory. Visitors may work remotely for offshore clients, and new migrants get a four-year foreign income exemption that excludes employment and services income.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed pay the ACC earners' levy (1.75%), an industry work levy (average NZD 0.69 per 100) and the Working Safer Levy (NZD 0.08 per 100): about 2.52% on average, to the same NZD 156,641 earnings cap. Full-time self-employed have an indicative minimum liable earnings of about NZD 48,000. KiwiSaver is optional.
income_tax.local_tax_note: No local income tax. The Inland Revenue page (updated June 2025, re-read 2026-10-15) lists the same bands as 'from 1 April 2025'; no 2026/27 change was found in the Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2026 summary (28 May 2026). ACC 2026/27: earners' levy 1.75% GST-inclusive to NZD 156,641 maximum earnings, work levy average NZD 0.69 per 100 (calculate.co.nz). KiwiSaver default 3.5% employee contribution, not counted.

regimes.name: Visitor visa remote work and non-resident visitor tax exemption
regimes.description: Visitor visas applied for from 27 January 2025 allow remote work for an employer or clients outside New Zealand. Inland Revenue's non-resident visitor category (from 1 April 2026) covers a visitor present up to 275 days in any 18-month period who is not a NZ tax resident or transitional resident, is not working for or paid by a NZ resident or NZ branch, does not sell to NZ customers, is not required to be in New Zealand for the work, is lawfully here and pays tax in a country where they are resident. Moore Markhams lists the income covered as employment income, services to non-resident persons and non-resident business income, so a remote worker's pay for work done while in New Zealand is exempt; work that requires physical presence in New Zealand, and work for NZ employers, is not. Counted as covering local work, but only for stays within the 275-day window.
regimes.duration_note: Up to 275 days within any 18-month period (Inland Revenue). Immigration NZ's visitor visa page separately cites 92 days (income taxed elsewhere) or 183 days (treaty country) as day thresholds where New Zealand tax may arise; the two are not reconciled. Visitor visa length itself not stated.

succession.name: New Zealand
succession.summary: There is no fixed share for children, but the Family Protection Act 1955 lets a court award a share to a spouse, partner, children and others, and the Property (Relationships) Act 1976 gives a surviving partner a choice between a relationship-property split and the will. New Zealand has its own Trusts Act 2019 but has not joined the Hague Trusts Convention. There is no private foundation.
succession.family_claims: Family Protection Act 1955 (claims by spouse/partner, children, step-children, grandchildren, parents in limited cases); Law Reform (Testamentary Promises) Act 1949; Property (Relationships) Act 1976 Part 8 (surviving partner's option to take a property split instead of the will).
succession.foreign_law_note: Succession to movables follows the deceased's last domicile and succession to land follows the law of its location (common-law conflict rules); there is no choice of law by nationality. Family Protection Act claims can apply to NZ-domiciled estates and to NZ land.
succession.trust_note: Trusts Act 2019 (in force 30 Jan 2021) codifies trust law; trusts can be foreign or domestic. NZ does not appear on the HCCH Convention table. Foreign trusts are recognised under common law rules. Foreign-sourced-income trusts have a special trust regime (non-resident trustee, foreign trust disclosure rules). No private foundation statute exists; charitable boards are incorporated under the Charitable Trusts Act 1957.

assumptions: The family are EU citizens with no job or business who become New Zealand tax residents with no residence in the previous 10 years, for example through the Active Investor Plus resident visa. They are therefore transitional residents for 4 years.

FIF income and tax are worked on the portfolio value at the start of the year. The year's total return is at least 5%, so a natural person's option to use the lower comparative value never applies. In a year of poor returns the personal paths would pay less, the company would not.
Both spouses are at the top rate of 39% (income above NZD 180,000); 5% of the portfolio is far above that for each. Allowances and lower brackets are ignored.

Foreign dividends carry 15% withholding, creditable in full: the treaty rate caps the credit at 15% and the New Zealand FIF tax on the same shares is higher. Source countries with a 30% or no-treaty withholding would not be credited above the treaty rate.

The revenue account method is not offered: it is limited to unlisted foreign shares, and its extended form (all listed shares) is for people taxed twice by citizenship or a right to work elsewhere, in practice US citizens. The EU family has a listed portfolio and no such double taxation.

A family trust is not a path: the trustee rate is 39%, so it offers no rate advantage over personal holding. A portfolio investment entity (PIE, investor tax capped at 28%) cannot normally be set up by a single family.
NZD 400,000 of annual spending is taken from the portfolio's own yield; the payout tax of the company is outside the annual figure.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: after the 4 transitional years a family could move the portfolio into a New Zealand company (the best New Zealand route in the long run: 1.4% instead of 1.95%) without having paid FIF tax before. The engine can only run one regime per path, with a time-limited one falling back to the standard personal rules, so 'transitional resident, then company' cannot be projected.

The company's running cost (NZD 10,000 a year, an unsourced estimate in the tax file) may not be deductible against FIF income: whether Income Tax Act 2007 allows a deduction for expenditure incurred in deriving FDR income was not established from an opened source. The check counts the cost in full and takes no deduction.

The transitional-resident exemption section (s CW 27) and the company rate and individual rate schedules (sch 1) were cited from general knowledge of the Income Tax Act 2007; the statute text on legislation.govt.nz was not opened. The exemption itself, the 48-month term and the FIF carve-out for transitional residents rest on IRD's IR461 and an IRD technical article found through search.

Budget 2026 FIF proposals (RAM for unlisted shares for all residents, extended RAM, de minimis NZD 100,000, from 1 April 2026) are not law as far as could be confirmed. They do not change this family's listed-share portfolio.

Revenue account method: the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2026-27, FBT Simplification, Foreign Investment Funds, and Remedial Measures) Bill was introduced on 10 September 2026 (KPMG NZ, EY); the tax file's regime text calls it law from 30 March 2026 with high confidence. Re-check its status; it does not affect this EU family's paths.

Comparative value method: individuals may pay on the lower of the 5% FDR and the actual return (floor zero); in years when the portfolio's total return is below 5% the tax is lower than modelled. Under the steady 7% return assumed here FDR is the lower.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally (foreign investment fund rules)
paths.note: There is no capital gains tax and no inheritance tax. A resident holding more than NZD 50,000 (cost) of foreign shares is taxed under the foreign investment fund rules on a deemed 5% of the opening market value (fair dividend rate), at the 39% top rate = 1.95% of the portfolio a year whatever it earns. Dividends and gains on those shares are not taxed separately; the foreign withholding tax is credited against the FIF tax (Income Tax Act 2007, subpart LJ).

paths.name: Transitional resident exemption (4 years), then personal holding
paths.note: A new resident who was not tax resident in the previous 10 years is exempt on foreign-sourced income for 4 years and outside the FIF rules; only New Zealand-source dividends are taxed. From year 5 the personal FIF rules apply. The exemption is automatic and once in a lifetime. The family keeps the portfolio in its own name during these years: a New Zealand company would pay FIF tax from day one.

paths.name: New Zealand investment holding company
paths.regime: New Zealand investment holding company (28% company tax on FIF income)
paths.note: A New Zealand company owns the portfolio and pays the FIF tax at the 28% company rate (5% x 28% = 1.4% of value) instead of 1.95%. Companies cannot use the comparative value method or the NZD 50,000 de minimis, so the 1.4% is paid even in a loss year. Distributions carry imputation credits for the 28% already paid, leaving 11 points at the 39% rate. The shares are in the parents' estate, but there is no inheritance tax. Not useful during the transitional years, and not for US persons.

immigration.name: New Zealand
immigration.summary: No free movement for EU citizens; EU, US and other passports use the same routes. Investors can get residence through Active Investor Plus: Growth (NZD 5 million for 3 years, 21 days in New Zealand) or Balanced (NZD 10 million for 5 years, 105 days). Workers use the Accredited Employer Work Visa. There is no digital nomad or retirement visa; visitors may work remotely for overseas employers for short stays.
immigration.naturalisation: Citizenship by grant needs a resident visa, 1,350 days in New Zealand in the 5 years before applying with at least 240 days in each year, plus language and character requirements (DIA). Residence by AIP counts only as time spent as a resident.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: New Zealand generally allows dual citizenship; not confirmed on a page read in this run.

routes.name: Active Investor Plus (AIP) resident visa - Growth
routes.summary: Residence for investing at least NZD 5 million for 3 years in New Zealand growth assets, with only 21 days in the country.
routes.requirements: Invest at least NZD 5 million for 36 months in direct investments, managed funds (and philanthropy up to 20%). At least 21 days in New Zealand as a resident over the 36 months. Permanent residence can be applied for after 3 years. Good health and character; police certificate under 6 months old; funds lawfully acquired; approval in principle within about 11 weeks for 80% of applications, then 6 months to transfer and invest; questionnaires at 24 months and at the end. Changes: philanthropy up to 20% of the Growth amount (May 2026); funding-source evidence rules changed 12 August 2026; from 28 September 2026 managed funds must provide deployment plans and a declined applicant waits 6 months to reapply (secondary summary).
routes.investment_options: Direct investments (including private equity and unlisted), managed funds, philanthropy up to 20% of the total.
routes.fees_note: Immigration New Zealand lists 'from NZD 27,470' (breakdown not read).
routes.processing_time: Approval in principle within 11 weeks for 80% of applications
routes.family: Partner (12 months' cohabitation) and dependent children aged 24 or younger; partner gets a visitor visa, children can apply for student visas.
routes.tax_note: Residents are taxed on worldwide income, but new migrants and returning residents may qualify for a 15-year foreign-income exemption (transitional resident rule; not verified here).

routes.name: Active Investor Plus (AIP) resident visa - Balanced
routes.summary: Residence for investing at least NZD 10 million for 5 years in a wider set of assets, including bonds and listed shares.
routes.requirements: Invest at least NZD 10 million for 60 months in direct investments, managed funds, listed equities, bonds, property developments and philanthropy. At least 105 days in New Zealand over 60 months; extra Growth funds reduce this (NZD 11 million 91 days, NZD 12 million 77, NZD 13 million 63; maximum cut 42 days). Permanent residence after 5 years. Good health and character; police certificate under 6 months old; funds lawfully acquired; approval in principle within about 11 weeks for 80% of applications, then 6 months to transfer and invest; questionnaires at 24 months and at the end. Changes: philanthropy up to 20% of the Growth amount (May 2026); funding-source evidence rules changed 12 August 2026; from 28 September 2026 managed funds must provide deployment plans and a declined applicant waits 6 months to reapply (secondary summary).
routes.investment_options: Direct investments, managed funds, listed equities, bonds, property developments, philanthropy.
routes.fees_note: Immigration New Zealand lists 'from NZD 27,470'; breakdown not read.
routes.physical_presence: 105 days over the 60-month period (reducible to 63 with NZD 13 million)
routes.processing_time: Approval in principle within 11 weeks for 80% of applications
routes.family: Partner (12 months' cohabitation) and dependent children aged 24 or younger; partner gets a visitor visa, children can apply for student visas.
routes.tax_note: Residents are taxed on worldwide income, subject to the transitional-resident exemption (not verified).

routes.name: Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV)
routes.summary: Employer-sponsored work visa for up to 5 years; the standard route for skilled workers.
routes.requirements: Full-time job (30+ hours) from an accredited employer with an approved job check; 2+ years' experience or a level 4 qualification unless paid at least NZD 67.12 an hour; English needed for skill levels 3-5; stay up to 5 years (3 years for skill level 4-5 jobs); no partner or children included in the application. Fee from NZD 1,540; 80% processed in 5 weeks. Can lead to residence through the Skilled Migrant Category.
routes.physical_presence: Live and work in NZ for the accredited employer
routes.family: Partner and children apply separately (not read in detail).

routes.name: Visitor visa / NZeTA with incidental remote work (no digital nomad visa)
routes.summary: New Zealand has no digital nomad visa, but visitor visas and NZeTA entries applied for from 27 January 2025 allow remote work for an overseas employer or clients.
routes.requirements: Work for a New Zealand employer, sales to New Zealand customers and jobs needing a physical workplace in NZ remain barred. Stay up to 3 months per visit on an NZeTA (6 months for UK passports), or up to 9 months in an 18-month period on a visitor visa. Tax: Taxation Act 2025 from 1 April 2026 may exempt short non-resident visits; 183-day rule still sets tax residence. Details from secondary sources.
routes.fees_note: NZeTA and visitor visa fees not recorded.
routes.physical_presence: Maximum 3 months per visit (NZeTA) or 9 months in 18 (visitor visa)
routes.tax_note: Staying over 183 days in any 12 months makes you a New Zealand tax resident.
